title: Pilate’s Praetorium: Trial Geography
subtitle: Textual headquarters, western-palace model, and Antonia-area tradition
summary: Compare the unlocated Gospel praetorium with the western Herodian palace model and the Antonia-area trial tradition without converting the modern Via Dolorosa into a recovered first-century route.
disclaimer: The Gospels place Jesus before Pilate at a praetorium in Jerusalem but do not supply a modern coordinate. The western Herodian palace is a major historical proposal; the Antonia-area location remains influential in later tradition. Neither model licenses an exact trial room, Gabbatha pavement, or recovered trial-to-Golgotha street route.

evidenceLegend.label: Physical geography
evidenceLegend.description: Established topography or measured terrain when a verified DEM is configured.

evidenceLegend.label: Known archaeology
evidenceLegend.description: Archaeological context represented only at the level supported by existing atlas records.

evidenceLegend.label: Historical inference
evidenceLegend.description: A historically reasoned reconstruction or orientation that is not an observed event location.

evidenceLegend.label: Tradition
evidenceLegend.description: A later Christian or local identification kept distinct from textual and archaeological certainty.

evidenceLegend.label: Unknown / disputed
evidenceLegend.description: An event point, route, building, or identification that cannot responsibly be fixed to one coordinate.

entryCamera.note: The initial camera frames western and eastern Jerusalem together so competing praetorium models can be compared; it is not the praetorium coordinate.

comparison.label: Where was Pilate’s Jerusalem praetorium?
comparison.intro: The textual location is real but unpinned. Compare the principal geographic models while keeping physical structures separate from the claim that the trial occurred there.

options.label: Textual praetorium
options.summary: The Gospels identify the governor’s headquarters by function/name but do not give a recoverable modern coordinate.
options.rationale: Starting from the text prevents either later model from being silently promoted to fact.
options.objections: A display camera is necessary for orientation, but it must not be read as the building’s location.

camera.note: Frames central Jerusalem only; neither praetorium nor Gabbatha is pinned by this camera.

options.label: Western palace model
options.summary: Herod’s palace complex on Jerusalem’s western hill is a major proposal for the governor’s temporary Jerusalem headquarters.
options.rationale: Roman governors could use royal/palatial accommodation, and the palace location is historically/topographically significant in the debate.
options.objections: The physical palace location does not prove that Jesus’ trial occurred at a specific room or pavement there.

camera.note: This camera locates the approximate western palace complex, not a recovered trial chamber.

options.label: Antonia-area tradition
options.summary: The Antonia fortress area is a real first-century topographic feature but its use as the site of Pilate’s trial is a separate traditional/historical claim.
options.rationale: The area became central to later Passion topography and the Via Dolorosa tradition.
options.objections: Knowing approximately where Antonia stood does not establish that it was the praetorium used by Pilate for this trial.

camera.note: This camera locates the approximate Antonia area; the trial identification remains traditional/disputed.

hotspots.label: Praetorium — textual, unlocated
hotspots.summary: The Gospel term names the governor’s headquarters but does not identify one recoverable modern building.

whyShown.inference: The point is a display anchor for the unresolved city-level question, not a site identification.

hotspots.label: Gabbatha / Lithostrotos — unlocated
hotspots.summary: John names Gabbatha but its modern position depends on the unresolved praetorium question.

whyShown.inference: This nearby display anchor exists solely to explain that no defensible coordinate is known.

hotspots.label: Herod’s western palace complex
hotspots.summary: A historically probable palace area and a major praetorium proposal, represented only as an approximate zone.

whyShown.evidence: The palace complex is historically/topographically well grounded as a broad area.
whyShown.inference: Its use as the specific Gospel praetorium is a historical proposal, not an excavated event association.

hotspots.label: Antonia fortress area
hotspots.summary: The fortress’s approximate physical location is historically significant; identifying it as Pilate’s trial site remains separate.

whyShown.evidence: The Antonia area is part of first-century Jerusalem topography.
whyShown.inference: The hotspot’s evidence class refers to its use in trial tradition, not to the existence of the fortress itself.
whyShown.alternatives: The western-palace model remains a major alternative.

hotspots.label: Modern Via Dolorosa ≠ recovered route
hotspots.summary: The devotional route is historically important but is not presented as a street-by-street recovery of Jesus’ movement from trial to crucifixion.

whyShown.evidence: Later Christian tradition developed a devotional Passion route through the city.
whyShown.inference: The marker is explanatory only; no exact first-century route polyline is drawn.
